lessons.title: Hydraulic principles and hazards
lessons.html:
What a pump must do

An irrigation pump adds energy to water so it can be lifted and pushed through pipes to the emitters at the right pressure. The total energy needed is expressed as total dynamic head (TDH) in metres:

  • Static suction lift or head: vertical distance from water level to the pump
  • Static delivery head: vertical distance from the pump to the highest outlet
  • Friction losses in pipes, fittings, valves and filters
  • Operating pressure required at the emitters (1 bar is about 10 m)

Each pump has a performance curve: as head increases, flow decreases. The operating point is where the pump curve crosses the system curve. Choose a pump whose best efficiency point is close to the required duty.

Suction and cavitation

Pumps cannot pull water; atmospheric pressure pushes it into the suction. The practical suction lift is limited and gets less at higher altitude, such as on the Highveld. If pressure at the pump inlet falls too low, water boils into vapour bubbles that collapse violently: cavitation. It sounds like gravel in the pump and erodes impellers. Avoid it by keeping suction lift low, suction pipes short and large enough, and ensuring the net positive suction head available exceeds that required by the pump.

Hazards and precautions

HazardPrecaution
ElectricityOnly qualified electricians work on motors and panels; lock out and tag out before mechanical work
Rotating shafts and couplingsKeep guards fitted; never run without them
Stored pressureIsolate valves and release pressure before opening
Heavy liftingUse slings, hoists and correct technique
Hot surfaces and enginesAllow to cool; fuel only with engine off
Water bodiesCare at dam and river intakes; never work alone near deep water
NoiseHearing protection near diesel engines

The OHS Act 85 of 1993 and its Driven Machinery Regulations require machinery to be guarded and safely maintained.

lessons.title: Types of irrigation pumps
lessons.html:
Two families of pumps

Pumps are grouped into dynamic (rotodynamic) pumps, which add velocity to water with a spinning impeller, and positive displacement pumps, which trap a fixed volume and push it out.

Dynamic pumps

TypeFeatures and use
End-suction centrifugalMost common surface irrigation pump; one impeller, suction at the end, delivery on top
Split-case centrifugalDouble-suction impeller, high flows, easy service; large pump stations
Multistage centrifugalSeveral impellers in series to build high pressure; booster sets, drip on long runs
Submersible borehole pumpMultistage pump with a sealed motor below water
Vertical turbineBowls below water driven from a surface motor; sumps and canals
Self-priming centrifugalHolds water in its casing to re-prime; wellpoints and small dams
Axial and mixed flowVery high flow, low head; flood and canal irrigation

Flow from a dynamic pump changes with head: throttling the delivery valve reduces flow. It can run briefly against a closed valve, but heats up quickly.

Positive displacement pumps

TypeFeatures and use
Piston (reciprocating) pumpHigh pressure, low flow; spray pumps, older windmill pumps
Diaphragm pumpChemical dosing and metering
Progressive cavity (helical rotor)Boreholes with low yield and high head; solar pumps
Gear and vane pumpsMainly hydraulics and fuel, sometimes small dosing

A positive displacement pump delivers nearly the same flow regardless of pressure. Never run it against a closed valve: pressure builds until something bursts. A pressure relief valve must protect it.

Choosing a pump

Consider the duty (flow and head), water source and quality, power source (Eskom, solar, diesel), efficiency, spares availability and service support in your area.

lessons.title: Mounting, servicing and documentation
lessons.html:
Mounting a pump on a concrete base

  1. Build a concrete plinth larger than the baseplate, level, above flood level, with holding-down bolts set in the right positions (or drilled anchors once cured).
  2. Place the pump and motor (on a common baseplate) and level it with shims.
  3. Align the coupling between pump and motor with a straight edge or dial gauge as the manufacturer specifies; misalignment destroys bearings and seals.
  4. Tighten the holding-down bolts and recheck alignment.

Suction manifold

  • Use a pipe larger than the pump inlet, with an eccentric reducer at the pump, flat side on top, so air pockets cannot form.
  • Slope suction pipe steadily upwards towards the pump; no high points.
  • Fit a foot valve with strainer below the lowest water level for lift installations, or an isolating valve for flooded suction.
  • Keep a straight length before the inlet, without elbows directly at the pump.
  • All joints must be airtight.

Delivery manifold

Concentric reducer, then pressure gauge, non-return valve, isolating (gate or butterfly) valve, air release valve, and connection to the mainline. Support pipes so their weight does not rest on the pump casing.

Servicing and maintenance

CheckInterval (typical)
Noise, vibration, leaks, gauge readings, motor temperatureDaily or each run
Gland packing drip or mechanical seal leakageWeekly
Bearing lubricationAs manufacturer specifies
Coupling alignment and rubber elementsEvery few months
Flow and pressure against commissioning valuesSeasonally
Impeller and wear ring inspectionWhen performance drops
Engine oil, filters, belts on diesel unitsPer engine hours

Documentation

  • Pump nameplate data, motor data, duty point and installation date
  • Commissioning flow, pressure and current readings
  • Maintenance log: date, hours run, work done, parts, readings
  • Faults and corrective action

Key points

  • Total dynamic head includes lift, delivery height, friction and emitter pressure.
  • Avoid cavitation with low suction lift and correctly sized, airtight suction pipes.
  • Never run a positive displacement pump against a closed valve.
  • Align couplings and use an eccentric reducer flat side up on the suction.
  • Lock out before work, keep guards on, and keep full records.
